periods.analysis: Procurement cycle time closed 2024-Q3 at 30 days, exactly on the <=30-day target and green, with no prior quarter in this series for comparison. That is acceptable performance, not excess capacity; at the target line, one late legal review or insurance certificate can move us into yellow. The strongest control this quarter was the Purchasing desk's daily triage of requisitions over $75,000, especially parks maintenance contracts and the Library RFID refresh purchase orders. I am treating this as a stable baseline, with limited tolerance for unmanaged exceptions.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the daily requisition aging report and require buyers to document the blocking reason by day 20 for any file not yet released. Extend the standard scope-of-work checklist to Facilities and Parks so repeat solicitations do not restart from blank templates. Keep Finance review authority centralized for high-risk vendors while allowing routine blanket purchase releases to proceed under the existing control matrix.

periods.analysis: Procurement cycle time improved to 28 days in 2024-Q4, down 2 days from 30, and remained green against the <=30-day target. The improvement came despite year-end volume, helped by pre-scheduled bid openings for fleet tires, janitorial supplies, and the Harborview Reads programming contracts. Controls held: no emergency-purchase clustering appeared in the December exception log, and Legal completed standard terms review within the agreed five-business-day lane. This is the right direction, but the margin is still narrow enough that we should not loosen documentation discipline.
periods.recommendations: Lock in the Q4 bid calendar practice by publishing the next two quarters of solicitation dates to departments by the first week of January. Sustain the Legal fast-lane for preapproved standard terms, and measure any deviation separately from buyer processing time. Add a spot check of three expedited files per month to confirm speed is not coming from incomplete insurance, W-9, or conflict-of-interest documentation.

periods.analysis: Procurement cycle time reached 23 days in 2025-Q1, improving 5 days from 28 and remaining green with meaningful room under the <=30-day target. This was the best quarter so far, and the improvement aligns with the January rollout of the Bonfire intake templates for IT peripherals, recreation instructors, and small construction task orders. The control benefit is important: cleaner intake reduced rework rather than simply pushing approvals faster. I view the 23-day result as strong, but it should be validated for sustainability before we reset any service-level expectations.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the Bonfire intake templates and extend them to Public Works operating supplies and Library materials vendors by quarter-end. Keep the 23-day result as an internal stretch benchmark, not a public service commitment, until we see two more quarters of similar performance. Run a post-award sample of ten Q1 files to verify that evaluation scoring, vendor debarment checks, and approval timestamps are complete.

periods.analysis: Procurement cycle time moved to 26 days in 2025-Q2, up 3 days from 23 but still green and comfortably within the <=30-day target. The increase is explainable: spring construction season brought heavier routing for sidewalk panels, signal cabinet parts, and beach-access maintenance contracts, many of which needed engineering signoff before award. I do not see a control failure in the movement, but I do see a capacity warning around technical review queues. The quarter remains healthy, provided we manage those queues before summer operating demand peaks.
periods.recommendations: Create a weekly Engineering-review queue with named alternates for procurements over $50,000 so technical approvals do not sit unassigned. Sustain the Bonfire templates that drove Q1 performance, but add discipline-specific attachments for construction and right-of-way work. Track the next quarter's files by delay source—department scope, Purchasing, Legal, Engineering, or vendor documents—so we know whether the 3-day increase is seasonal or structural.

periods.analysis: Procurement cycle time rose again to 29 days in 2025-Q3, up 3 days from 26, while still green under the <=30-day target. This is the second consecutive increase, and at 29 days we are one day from the threshold, so I am not going to call this comfortable. The main pressure points were summer recreation vendor renewals, police radio accessories, and several coastal resilience design procurements that required insurance endorsements and federal-terms review. Performance is technically green, but the risk posture is watchful because the buffer has narrowed.
periods.recommendations: Hold a two-week procurement recovery sprint focused on files aged 24 days or more, with Purchasing, Legal, and Risk Management reviewing the same queue each morning. Sustain the green result by preserving competitive controls, but require department directors to approve any scope change after solicitation release. Prepare a Q4 renewal calendar for recurring contracts so recreation, public safety, and coastal projects are not all entering the same approval lane at once.

periods.analysis: Procurement cycle time improved to 26 days in 2025-Q4, down 3 days from 29, returning us to a safer green position below the <=30-day target. The Q3 recovery sprint appears to have worked: aged files dropped after we separated routine renewals from complex solicitations and assigned Risk Management review earlier for marine contractors. Year-end purchasing remained controlled, with blanket purchase order renewals for office supplies, custodial chemicals, and fleet parts processed through the pre-clearance list. This quarter restores margin, but the lesson is clear: green performance depends on active queue management, not luck.
periods.recommendations: Make the aged-file recovery sprint a standing monthly control, triggered automatically when any procurement reaches 24 days. Extend the pre-clearance list to recurring software renewals and low-risk professional services where terms have not changed. Continue director-level review of late scope changes, and report exceptions separately so cycle time gains do not mask avoidable department rework.

periods.analysis: Procurement cycle time improved further to 24 days in 2026-Q1, down 2 days from 26, and remained green against the <=30-day target. The result reflects maturing controls: the monthly aged-file review, earlier Risk Management routing, and standard renewal packets reduced avoidable handoffs. We also benefited from the January vendor-document cleanup, where Purchasing corrected expired certificates for the top 40 recurring vendors before requisitions were submitted. This is strong performance with a defensible control trail, which is the combination I want.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the vendor-document cleanup as a quarterly preflight, beginning with vendors tied to public safety, utilities, and resident-facing programs. Extend standard renewal packets to grant-funded purchases so federal clauses are attached at intake rather than late in review. Add a dashboard flag for files with more than two department revisions, because repeated scope edits are the next controllable risk.

periods.analysis: Procurement cycle time finished 2026-Q2 at 25 days, up 1 day from 24, still green and well within the <=30-day target. A one-day increase is not material by itself, especially during spring bid activity for pavement markings, marina restroom repairs, and summer camp transportation, but it is still worth noting. The controls put in place since 2024-Q3 are producing a better operating range: we moved from 30 days to a stable mid-20s pattern without sacrificing documentation. Harborview is growing quickly, and this measure shows the procurement function can support that growth if we keep capacity and review discipline aligned.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the monthly aged-file review and quarterly vendor preflight as permanent controls, with results included in the Finance & Administration scorecard packet. Extend the department revision dashboard to show the top five delay causes and assign corrective action owners before the next quarter closes. For green sustainability, pilot category-specific procurement calendars for construction, recreation, and technology so seasonal demand is planned before requisitions enter the queue.

periods.analysis: The available cycle time is 34 days, four days above the 30-day ceiling. It conflicts with the earlier narrative describing a 25-day result, so the source spreadsheet needs checking before we attribute a cause or call this a September deterioration.
periods.recommendations: Validate the cycle-time extract, review aged requisitions and vendor onboarding delays, and bring a corrected source record or a recovery plan to the next review.
